I have been farming this land for 15 years now and the system I use has not changed much — wheat in winter, maize in summer on the main fields, and then chili and stevia as my cash crops on the side plots. 225 mu is a lot to manage but I know every section of it by now.

My main rotation land is about 150 mu. That goes wheat then maize, same as always, same as my neighbors. The other 75 mu I split — 40 mu for chili and 35 mu for stevia. Stevia I keep because the contract buyer comes every year and the price is stable. Chili is riskier but if the market is good I make more per mu than wheat ever gives me.

**Wheat:** I plough in September, put down the base fertilizer before sowing. Last year I used about 40 kg of diammonium phosphate plus 25 kg urea per mu at base, then topped up with another 10 kg urea at jointing. That is roughly 18 kg nitrogen and 7 kg phosphorus total. My neighbor who skimped on nitrogen the year before last had thin stems and lodging — I am not doing that. I irrigate 4 times: once in winter to protect roots, then jointing, heading, and grain fill. Three pesticide rounds — herbicide early winter, powdery mildew spray in April, aphid spray before harvest.

**Maize:** Right after wheat harvest I do no-till direct seeding, mostly Xianyu 335 hybrid seed. I have used it for 5 years and know what to expect from it. Nitrogen I split — 8 kg base with compound fertilizer, then chase with another 10 kg urea at 8-leaf stage. Phosphorus and potassium I mostly front-load. Two irrigations, one at tasseling, one at grain fill if it is dry. Two pesticide rounds — corn borer spray and one fungicide if there is leaf blight pressure.

**Chili:** This crop drinks water and eats fertilizer. I put in rotary tillage and base compound fertilizer before transplanting. Chili needs potassium or the fruit is small and the color is bad — I put 9 kg K per mu total across the season. I irrigate 6 times, drip if I can manage it on this plot since it saves water from the well. Four pesticide rounds minimum — aphids come every year and anthracnose ruins the fruit if I miss the window.

**Stevia:** This is relatively easy to manage. It is a perennial but I treat it like an annual crop, cutting twice a year. I do rotary tillage in spring to loosen the soil around the roots. It does not need as much fertilizer as chili. Two pesticide rounds, mostly preventive. I irrigate 4 times through the season.

The well can handle all this — I have a pump and the water table is okay in this part of Quzhou. My big worry this year is fertilizer prices. If they go up again I will have to cut somewhere, probably the stevia gets a bit less, because that crop is forgiving.
